summary: Adds guidelines for benchmarking IPv6 performance of network interconnect devices such as routers, to be used together with RFC 2544. RFC 2544 is independent of IP version but misses some IPv6 specifics. Transition mechanisms are out of scope. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This paper is a speed-test guide for IPv6 equipment. It adds to an older test guide so network boxes can be measured fairly with the newer addresses.

questions: what is the ipv6 benchmarking address block
subtitle: Extra rules for speed-testing routers and similar devices with IPv6 traffic, layered on top of RFC 2544.

tldr.problem: RFC 2544 benchmarking is largely IP version independent but does not cover IPv6 specifics such as extension headers, IPv6 addressing and neighbor discovery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC keeps the RFC 2544 tests and adds IPv6 guidance on frame sizes, the benchmark address block, extension header chains, filters, and IPv4/IPv6 traffic mixes.
tldr.outcome: It complements RFC 2544 and does not replace it. The back-to-back frames test is no longer recommended for IPv6, and IPv6 transition mechanisms are out of scope.

today: RFC 5180 is an Informational document published in May 2008. The unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, and the text says it complements RFC 2544 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: Extending RFC 2544 to IPv6
sections.content:
The methods in RFC 2544 help compare the forwarding performance of network elements objectively. Their principles are largely IP version independent, but IPv6 has specifics that RFC 2544 does not address, such as traffic with extension headers.

RFC 5180 defines recommendations within the RFC 2544 framework. Terms stay consistent with RFC 1242, and anything not covered here SHOULD be treated as RFC 2544 recommends. Results should follow generally accepted practice for repeatability, variance and statistical significance. Not every test applies to every kind of network element.
sections.eli5: There is already a rulebook for timing network boxes. This new page adds rules for the newer kind of address, and says to use the old rulebook for everything else.

sections.title: Test Setup and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
The setup is the same as in Section 6 of RFC 2544, in both single-port and multi-port scenarios. Single-port tests measure per-interface forwarding, and multi-port tests measure how performance scales across the platform. The Device Under Test (DUT) can be monitored for processor and memory use, which could show whether IPv6 is handled in hardware or punted to the software path. That data MUST be collected out of band.

Neighbor information can be configured statically or discovered dynamically. Dynamic discovery is preferred, with the test tool keeping the neighbor caches active. To avoid neighbor solicitation and advertisement storms from neighbor unreachability detection, test traffic should simulate end points one hop beyond the DUT. When neighbors are not static, the prefix-reachable time in the router advertisement SHOULD be set to 30 seconds.
sections.eli5: The box being tested is watched quietly from the side. The test machine and the box can either be told each other's addresses by hand or learn them by chatting.

sections.title: Test Traffic: Frame Sizes and Addresses
sections.content:
On Ethernet, these frame sizes SHOULD be used: 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280 and 1518 bytes. For Packet over SONET, they are 47, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280, 1518, 2048 and 4096 bytes. Jumbo frames should be tested at sizes the device supports. The minimum IPv6 packet (40 bytes) is larger than an IPv4 one (20 bytes), and tests should compensate.

IANA has allocated 2001:0200::/48 for IPv6 benchmarking, and these addresses MUST NOT be used as Internet source or destination addresses. Source addresses SHOULD come from one half of the range and destinations from the other. DUT interface prefix lengths MUST be /126 or /64 and shorter, and global unicast Interface IDs SHOULD be ::1. Tests should be repeated with destination prefix lengths of 48, 64, 126 and 128, first with one address pair and then with random destinations.
sections.eli5: The test sends packets of many different sizes, from tiny to big, using a special set of addresses that is set aside just for testing so it never mixes with real traffic.

sections.title: Traffic with Extension Headers
sections.content:
All tests SHOULD be run both without and with IPv6 extension headers. Each header type SHOULD be tested individually. The hop-by-hop header is special because every forwarding node must process it, so it tests the DUT's header processing rather than throughput. It should be sent at 1%, 10% and 50% of the interface bandwidth while device resources are monitored.

Tests must also use a chain of two or more headers that excludes hop-by-hop. The chain should also exclude ESP, since an encrypted payload cannot be used with filters on upper-layer information. The recommended chain is a routing header of 24-32 bytes, a destination options header of 8 bytes and a fragment header of 8 bytes, with a total length larger than 32 bytes.

Extension header cost mostly shows up only when filters match on upper-layer information, because then the DUT must walk the chain. Bi-directional traffic SHOULD be used, and uni-directional traffic MAY be used for asymmetric cases.
sections.eli5: Some packets carry extra labels stuck on the front. The test tries packets with none, with each label alone, and with a stack of labels, to see if the box slows down.

sections.title: Modifiers, Filters and Tests
sections.content:
The RFC 2544 conditions apply, except that IPv6 has no layer 2 or 3 broadcasts. The suite is first run without modifiers and then repeated under each one. Filters use the format [permit|deny] [protocol] [SA] [DA], where protocol is ipv6, tcp or udp, and are tested as a single filter and as a set of 25 filters.

The tests are throughput, latency, frame loss, system recovery and reset, each with the same procedure and reporting as RFC 2544. The back-to-back frames test is no longer recommended for IPv6 because of its significant variance. Tests MUST be repeated for IPv6 with no extension headers, with one, and with the chain. Coexistence runs cover IPv4 only, IPv6 only, and IPv4/IPv6 mixes of 90%/10%, 50%/50% and 10%/90%.
sections.eli5: The box is timed on how many packets it passes, how long they take, how many it drops, and how fast it recovers from trouble. Then everything is tried again with filters and with old and new traffic mixed.

sections.title: Security and Lab Isolation
sections.content:
Benchmarking is limited to controlled laboratory tests with dedicated address space. The test network MUST NOT be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the test management network. Testing is black-box, using only measurements outside the DUT, and special benchmarking-only capabilities SHOULD NOT exist in the device. The RFC concludes that no security considerations specific to benchmarking arise from this isolation.

The RFC does not recommend Unique Local Addresses for testing, to minimize conflicts with operational traffic.
sections.eli5: The test lab is a closed room. Nothing from the test should leak out to the real network.
